newsitem.title: USA: Ill House advances rainy day fund legislation.
newsitem.headline: Ill House advances rainy day fund legislation.

text.p: The Illinois House late Wednesday passed legislation to establish a rainy day fund for the state, although a companion bill in the state Senate remains in committee.

Representatives approved the legislation 103-5 to create a fund to put away a portion of new base revenues for future economic emergencies, said Ed Marshall, spokesman for state Comptroller Loleta Didrickson, who wrote the legislation.
"While this year the state was upgraded by Moody's, the bond rating house cited our lack of a "rainy day" fund as a potential roadblock to future bond upgrades," Didrickson said in a news release.

Illinois is one of only four states that does not have a revenue stabilization fund, commonly refered to as a rainy day fund. Michigan recently completed an appropriation that raised the balance in its fund to more than $1 billion.

Under the proposal, if the governor predicts that general state revenues will exceed the prior fiscal year's base revenues by more than 4 percent, then the governor will recommend moving at least 0.25 percent of the estimated increase into the revenue stabilization fund.
If the rainy day fund reaches $350 million, any savings above that level would then go to finance schools under the proposal, Marshall noted.

Under current revenue estimates, no money would be contributed to the fund in fiscal year 1998, Marshall said. Had the fund been established in fiscal year 1995, however, then it could have reached the $350 million level by 2003, he noted.
Rep. Jeff Schoenberg, D-Evanston, was the chief sponsor of the legislation in the House. With the House passage, the bill will be refered to the Senate rules committee.
